title: Criminal and Civil Law
objective: After this level you can compare criminal and civil cases.
summary: Criminal cases are brought by the state and can end in punishment; civil cases settle disputes between people or organisations, usually with damages, and need only 'more likely than not'.

cards.headline: Acquitted in 1995. Found liable in 1997. Same man, same two deaths.
cards.body: In 1995 a jury acquitted O.J. Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. In 1997 a different jury, in a civil trial, found him liable for their deaths and ordered him to pay $33.5 million in damages to the families. A contradiction? No. Two different kinds of case, asking two different questions.

cards.headline: Criminal: the state brings the case
cards.body: A criminal case is about an alleged crime. It comes to court when the state decides to prosecute; in England and Wales that decision is usually the Crown Prosecution Service's. If the accused is convicted, the sentence can be prison, community punishment or a fine. The victim isn't suing anyone. The state is the one asking for punishment.

cards.headline: Civil: people versus people
cards.body: A civil case is a dispute between people, businesses or organisations: damaged goods, say, or an unpaid debt. Nobody goes to prison for losing. The winner may get damages, meaning money, or a court order telling someone to do or stop doing something. It's less "you broke the law" and more "you owe me".

cards.headline: Two different bars
cards.body: Here's the key. Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil claim needs only to be more likely than not: the balance of probabilities, anything over 50%. So a jury can have a reasonable doubt that Simpson committed murder, while another decides it's more likely than not he was responsible. Same facts, two bars, two answers.

mascot.line: Criminal and civil get mixed up. The quickest tell is the bar: reasonable doubt, or more likely than not.

cards.headline: Criminal vs civil
learned: Criminal: the state prosecutes a crime

questions.prompt: What does the winning side usually get in a civil case?

options.label: A prison sentence for the other side
options.rationale: Nobody goes to prison for losing a civil case.

options.label: The right to prosecute the other side
A criminal record for the other side
options.rationale: Civil cases don't create criminal convictions.

questions.explanation: In a civil case, the winner may get damages (money) or a court order.

questions.prompt: How could O.J. Simpson be acquitted in a criminal trial but found liable in a civil one?

options.label: The civil trial found new DNA evidence
options.rationale: The key difference is the standard of proof.

options.label: The civil case needed only "more likely than not", a lower bar
The criminal verdict was overturned on appeal
options.rationale: The acquittal stood; the civil case was separate.

options.label: Civil juries don't need to hear evidence
options.rationale: Civil juries weigh evidence too, just against a lower bar.

questions.explanation: Criminal guilt needs proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil liability needs only the balance of probabilities.

questions.prompt: Level 54's standard, proof beyond reasonable doubt, applies to which kind of case?

options.label: Civil cases over debts
options.rationale: Civil cases use the balance of probabilities.

options.label: Every case that reaches a court
options.rationale: Civil cases use a lower standard.

options.label: Only cases with a jury of 12
options.rationale: The standard depends on the kind of case, not the jury.

options.label: Criminal cases, where the state seeks punishment

questions.explanation: Beyond reasonable doubt is the criminal standard; civil cases need only the balance of probabilities.
